\chapter{Places --- and the Two Noun Families}
\label{ch:sa-places}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five places in Sanskrit, put a known adjective in front of any of them, and hear from a noun's ending whether it is neuter or masculine.}

Complete SA-C16-noun-families: sort the chapter's five places into the -am and -aH families and say a known adjective before each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gṛham]{\sk{गृहम्} (gṛham) — house, home}

\label{lesson:SA-C16-house}



\begin{quote}
You can describe a thing now — big, small, new, old. This chapter gives you places to put those things.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{गृहम्}}
\textbf{\sk{गृहम्}} (\emph{gṛham}) — \textquotedblleft{}house, home.\textquotedblright{}

The traditional derivation ties it to the root \textbf{√\sk{ग्रह्}} (\emph{grah}), \textquotedblleft{}to seize, to hold.\textquotedblright{} A house is \emph{the thing that holds you} — the grasp you live inside. That is how Sanskrit's own grammarians heard the word, and it is worth hearing that way.

You can already stack an adjective in front of it: \sk{महत्} \sk{गृहम्}, \textquotedblleft{}a big house\textquotedblright{}; \sk{नव} \sk{गृहम्}, \textquotedblleft{}a new house.\textquotedblright{} The adjective comes first, as you have already seen it do.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This is your first \textbf{place}. Everything in this chapter is somewhere you can be, and every one of them takes the adjectives you already own.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gṛham} — \textquotedblleft{}house\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a big house\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mahat gṛham}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a new house\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nava gṛham}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root is \sk{गृहम्} traditionally tied to? (√\sk{ग्रह्}, \textquotedblleft{}to seize, to hold.\textquotedblright{}) Where does the adjective go? (Before the noun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[grāmaḥ]{\sk{ग्रामः} (grāmaḥ) — village}

\label{lesson:SA-C16-village}



\begin{quote}
One house is a home. Many of them together are this.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{ग्रामः}}
\textbf{\sk{ग्रामः}} (\emph{grāmaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}village.\textquotedblright{}

Its oldest sense is not \textquotedblleft{}village\textquotedblright{} but \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}a collection, a troop\textquotedblright{}} — a gathering of people considered as one body. The settlement took its name from the group, not the group from the settlement, which tells you how the word's first speakers saw the place: people first, buildings after.

Notice the ending. \sk{गृहम्} ends in \emph{-am}; \sk{ग्रामः} ends in \emph{-aḥ}. Sanskrit sorts its nouns into families, and that final syllable is the badge. You do not need the system yet — only the observation that the endings differ, and that the difference is not random.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two places now, and your first glimpse of the noun families — the \emph{-am} ending and the \emph{-aḥ} ending, sitting side by side.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{grāmaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}village\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a big village\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mahat grāmaḥ}
  \item the two endings back to back — \emph{gṛham}, \emph{grāmaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \sk{ग्रामः} mean before it meant \textquotedblleft{}village\textquotedblright{}? (A collection, a troop.) Which two endings have you now seen? (\emph{-am} and \emph{-aḥ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṇa]{\sk{ण} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S217-letter-nna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{उ} · \sk{ष} · \sk{◌ौ}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ण}}
\textbf{\sk{ण}} — \emph{ṇa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ṇ}, it is \textbf{ṇa}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a joined left stem, clockwise lower bowl, and inner right stem
  \item a separate top-to-bottom outer right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{ण} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{कर्णः}} \emph{karṇaḥ} — ear — a word Sanskrit itself never settled the origin of
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ण}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the left stem's headline junction, descend, curve clockwise around the lower bowl, and rise along the inner right stem back to the headline without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the outer right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified three-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{ण}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{ण} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{कर्णः}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ण} three times, saying \emph{ṇa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{ण} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{ण}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ṇa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mārgaḥ]{\sk{मार्गः} (mārgaḥ) — road, path}

\label{lesson:SA-C16-road}



\begin{quote}
Two places, and no way between them. Here is the way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मार्गः}}
\textbf{\sk{मार्गः}} (\emph{mārgaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}road, path, way.\textquotedblright{}

From the root √\sk{मृग्} (\emph{mṛg}), \textquotedblleft{}to track, to hunt, to search out.\textquotedblright{} A road is a \textbf{tracking} — the line left by someone who went looking. The same root gives \sk{मृगः} (\emph{mṛgaḥ}), \textquotedblleft{}deer\textquotedblright{}: the animal that gets tracked.

So the word does not name a built thing at all. It names the trace of a search, and only later the paved version of it. English keeps that metaphor alive when it speaks of a \emph{line of enquiry}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{\sk{मार्गः}} takes the same \emph{-aḥ} ending as \emph{\sk{ग्रामः}}. That is the second word in its family, and the pattern is becoming visible rather than asserted.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mārgaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}road\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}the old road\textquotedblright{} — \emph{purātana mārgaḥ}
  \item the related animal — \emph{mṛgaḥ}, \textquotedblleft{}deer\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does √\sk{मृग्} mean? (To track, to hunt.) What animal shares the root? (\sk{मृगः}, the deer.) Which ending does \sk{मार्गः} take? (\emph{-aḥ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vanam]{\sk{वनम्} (vanam) — forest, wood}

\label{lesson:SA-C16-forest}



\begin{quote}
Follow the road far enough out of the village and you reach this.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वनम्}}
\textbf{\sk{वनम्}} (\emph{vanam}) — \textquotedblleft{}forest, wood, wilderness.\textquotedblright{}

In the older literature it carries a weight that \textquotedblleft{}forest\textquotedblright{} does not quite catch: \emph{\sk{वनम्}} is where the settled world stops. To go to the \emph{\sk{वनम्}} is to leave the \emph{\sk{ग्रामः}} behind, and a great deal of Sanskrit narrative turns on somebody doing exactly that.

Its ending is \emph{-am}, so it belongs with \sk{गृहम्} — which gives the chapter a neat symmetry: the two \emph{-am} words so far are the house you live inside and the wild you do not.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four places, and the two endings now have two words each. That is a pattern you have observed, not one you have been handed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vanam} — \textquotedblleft{}forest\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a big forest\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mahat vanam}
  \item the two \emph{-am} words together — \emph{gṛham}, \emph{vanam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{वनम्} mean beyond \textquotedblleft{}forest\textquotedblright{}? (Where the settled world stops.) Which other word shares its ending? (\sk{गृहम्}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ga]{\sk{ग} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S218-letter-ga}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{ष} · \sk{◌ौ} · \sk{ण}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ग}}
\textbf{\sk{ग}} — \emph{ga}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{g}, it is \textbf{ga}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a counterclockwise left loop joined to an ascending stem
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{ग} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{स्वागतम्}} \emph{svāgatam} — welcome (lit. \textquotedblleft{}well come\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\sk{गृह्णाति}} \emph{gṛhṇāti} — he, she, or it takes, seizes — the ninth class again, and the root English grabs with
  \item \textbf{\sk{भगिनी}} \emph{bhaginī} — sister — not built on English \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{}'s root at all, but on \textquotedblleft{}one with a share\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\sk{गृहम्}} \emph{gṛham} — house, home
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ग}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the loop's upper-right junction and sweep left over the top, down around the left side, back to the lower-right junction, and continue up the joined stem to the headline
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified three-stroke teaching form; everyday handwriting may join or simplify the body differently
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{ग}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 9 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{ग} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{स्वागतम्}  ·  \sk{गृह्णाति}  ·  \sk{भगिनी}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ग} three times, saying \emph{ga} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{ग} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{ग}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ga}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nagaram]{\sk{नगरम्} (nagaram) — city}

\label{lesson:SA-C16-city}



\begin{quote}
The last of the five places, and the biggest.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{नगरम्}}
\textbf{\sk{नगरम्}} (\emph{nagaram}) — \textquotedblleft{}city, town.\textquotedblright{}

Its origin is \textbf{genuinely unsettled}, and that is worth saying plainly rather than inventing a story. Sanskrit offers no agreed root for it. Some scholars have proposed that it came into the language from outside — one of a handful of everyday words that may record a borrowing from languages spoken in the subcontinent before Sanskrit arrived. Others resist that reading. The honest position is that nobody knows.

Whatever its history, it ends in \emph{-am}, like \emph{\sk{गृहम्}} and \emph{\sk{वनम्}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five places: house, village, road, forest, city. Three take \emph{-am} and two take \emph{-aḥ}, and the next lesson says what that division actually is.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nagaram} — \textquotedblleft{}city\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a new city\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nava nagaram}
  \item all three \emph{-am} words — \emph{gṛham}, \emph{vanam}, \emph{nagaram}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is \sk{नगरम्} unusual among this chapter's words? (Its origin is unsettled; it may be a borrowing.) Which ending does it take? (\emph{-am}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-am · -aḥ]{-\sk{अम्} · -\sk{अः} (-am · -aḥ) — the two noun endings, side by side}

\label{lesson:SA-C16-noun-families}



\begin{quote}
You have met five places and noticed their endings differ. This lesson names what you noticed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: -\sk{अम्} · -\sk{अः}}
Sanskrit sorts its nouns into \textbf{genders}, and the ending you have been hearing is the clue:

\emph{\sk{गृहम्}}, \emph{\sk{वनम्}}, \emph{\sk{नगरम्}} end in -\sk{अम्} — these are \textbf{neuter}. \emph{\sk{ग्रामः}}, \emph{\sk{मार्गः}} end in -\sk{अः} — these are \textbf{masculine}.

This is the same machinery the adjectives used without naming it: they change to match. \emph{\sk{महत्} \sk{गृहम्}} and \emph{\sk{महान्} \sk{ग्रामः}} are one adjective agreeing with two different families.

You do not need to produce that agreement yet. What you need is the ear for it — when you hear \emph{-\sk{अम्}} or \emph{-\sk{अः}} closing a word, you are hearing which family it belongs to, and Sanskrit will keep using that information for everything that follows.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now hear a noun's family from its ending, which is the single most useful thing to know about a Sanskrit noun.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three neuters — \emph{gṛham}, \emph{vanam}, \emph{nagaram}
  \item the two masculines — \emph{grāmaḥ}, \emph{mārgaḥ}
  \item which family a new word ending in \emph{-am} belongs to
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending marks the neuter? (\emph{-\sk{अम्}}.) Which marks the masculine? (\emph{-\sk{अः}}.) What else in the sentence responds to a noun's family? (The adjective.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ja]{\sk{ज} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S120-letter-ja}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{◌ौ} · \sk{ण} · \sk{ग}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ज}}
\textbf{\sk{ज}} — \emph{ja}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{j}, it is \textbf{ja}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item an open left hook curling clockwise around the lower bowl and continuing through the middle bar
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{ज} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{जानाति}} \emph{jānāti} — he, she, or it knows — the root \sk{ज्ञा}, the class that plants a syllable inside the verb, and the chapter's six roots gathered up
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ज}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the open upper-left tip, sweep down and clockwise around the lower bowl, then rise through the inner shoulder and continue right along the middle bar to the right-stem junction without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{ज}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
